meetings.headline: Committee says it won't choose between a full-time athletic director and reading interventionists in FY27.
meetings.summary: The School Committee heard a select-board letter on tri-board communication, extensive public comment on reading support and the athletic director's workload, and then held a long FY27 budget workshop covering health insurance, a paraprofessional undercount in FY26, reading interventionists, EL staffing and the bridge program. Members declined to choose between funding a full-time athletic director/trainer and reading interventionists, agreed to make no further staffing cuts, planned to vote their own budget before the town manager's number arrives, and approved (pending edits) an official statement on FY2025 budget variances.

what_happened.line: The committee said it cannot sustain further staffing cuts and would not choose between a full-time athletic director/trainer and reading interventionists in the FY27 budget.
Members plan to vote their own FY27 school budget before the town manager sets her budget number, a change in sequencing from past years.
Any override request would go to the May town meeting rather than a November special town meeting, because November needs a higher approval threshold.
The committee voted to finalize its FY2025 budget variance statement, pending edits sent to the superintendent that do not change its message.
Officials disclosed a paraprofessional staffing gap in the current FY26 budget that had gone unaccounted for, but said the year should still close out okay.

why_it_matters: The choice between a full-time athletic director and reading interventionists is left open, so families may not know until later in the FY27 process which program gets funded.

An override, if requested, would appear on the May town meeting warrant rather than a November special vote, and this cycle's cuts would be discussed in broad categories rather than naming specific positions.
A paraprofessional undercount already found in the FY26 budget is a data gap worth watching for whether it recurs or grows in the FY27 numbers that underlie any override ask.

Two routine policies (middle school pathway exploration; competency determination) passed on third read, and Turkey Hill accessibility needs were flagged as needing near-term attention regardless of the MSBA timeline.

The school calendar presented tonight is a first draft; it will go to principals/school councils and be posted publicly for feedback before a vote.

The district will pursue a Massachusetts School Building Authority statement of intent for Turkey Hill targeting an April 2027 (not April 2026) submission.
The chair said the committee will wait for the MSBA process rather than pursue a competitive application this year.
The town's unused debt capacity (as distinct from a debt exclusion) and capital strategy will be discussed at the next tri-board meeting.
Mandy was designated to reach out to other (non-regional, similarly sized) school committees to explore a shared advocacy coalition on state funding.
The next tri-board meeting date has not yet been set; staff will follow up to schedule it.
Staff will try to compile a list of lower-cost Turkey Hill accessibility upgrades, likely by January, to scope near-term spending options.

meetings.headline: District previews FY27-29 outlook, asking to restore staff cut in FY26; no vote was taken.
meetings.summary: The select board, finance committee and school committee met jointly to hear a preliminary, forward-looking FY27-29 school budget outlook, explicitly deferring any FY25 questions to a later public forum. The superintendent and business manager walked through contractual assumptions (salaries, health insurance, utilities, transportation) and a series of requested staff restorations -- interventionists, a kindergarten paraprofessional, a world-language teacher, a music teacher, a bridge/TLC program, an ELL teacher, and a debated full-time athletic director/assistant principal split -- framed as restoring FY26 cuts rather than new expansion. No formal votes were taken on any budget item; the boards adjourned after discussion, with several follow-up items assigned to the administration for the next budget cycle.

budget_items.what_was_said: The district assumed a 20% annual health insurance increase for FY27 through FY29, projecting a large rise from FY23 actuals.
Electricity costs were shown rising from FY23 to a much higher FY29 projection, tied to a locked-in per-kWh rate with the district's provider.
Heating costs were projected lower than electricity and are currently under review for possible savings.
The transportation contract is described as effectively uncompetitive since no other vendor has bid in years, making the cost locked in regardless of market forces.

Of the two new high school positions, only one carries a health insurance cost since the other is already part-time with insurance.
Adding one van with a monitor to a transportation route that can't be regionalized for two students was cited as a striking cost example.
A guesstimated salary range was given for making the athletic director position full-time again.
The athletic director was previously paid as a stipend rather than a full position, cited to contrast with the current full-time ask.

Eliminating the reading coach and converting the math coach to a partly direct-service instructional specialist role was costed as a small net add, since the individual would move to the teachers' contract.

meetings.summary: The committee reviewed FY25 year-end finances and a growing surplus, accepted donations, and voted to raise substitute teacher pay to match regional rates. It revised the FY27 capital plan, discussed pursuing state building assistance for Turkey Hill Elementary, and heard the superintendent's preliminary FY27 budget memo, which restores several paraprofessional, interventionist, and other positions cut in recent years. A proposed cashless athletics-campus policy was sent back to the policy subcommittee after resident feedback, and a member raised concern that the school budget's health insurance line makes its year-over-year increase look larger than other town departments'.

The bulk of the meeting covered an assessment/accountability report showing concerning third-grade reading and special-education scores linked partly to prior budget cuts, followed by the superintendent's FY28 budget priorities, her first-year evaluation goals, and a discussion setting draft committee goals around Turkey Hill's future, capital planning, and a more reasoned budget-decision process.

budget_items.what_was_said: The parent-teacher organization donated funds to each school, left to each principal's discretion, and the committee voted to accept three such donations.
The superintendent described a one-time, non-recurring earmark from state legislators that cannot be added to the base budget; the captions gave inconsistent figures for the total and its two pieces.
The superintendent proposed spending part of the earmark on touch screens for every primary school classroom, the only school without them, replacing projectors.
The superintendent proposed restoring I-Ready diagnostic and instructional access for at least one more year; asked the cost, she said it was about 47.

The district considered using the earmark for smaller transportation vans instead, but determined the cost would exceed the available money and require driver stipends and special licenses, so it was not pursued.
Members noted the athletic fee was previously increased and is intended to partially cover uniform costs, though it does not cover the full cost.

The district previously cut a single dedicated Wilson reading position at Turkey Hill and instead used training funds to certify multiple inclusion teachers district-wide in the Wilson reading system.

Members discussed that compensation, especially for paraprofessionals, is weak compared to other districts, making positions hard to fill, though the superintendent cited staff loyalty to Lunenburg as a mitigating factor.

budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent set a goal of 90% or higher staff retention; last year's rate, which included layoffs, was described as concerningly low.
A member asked about anticipated multi-year budget impacts as union contracts, capped at three-year terms, come up for renewal; the business manager is building this into the long-term forecast.
The superintendent said she is conservatively forecasting entitlement grant funding to come in lower next year given uncertainty at the federal level.

budget_items.what_was_said: A member cited a prior renovation estimate for Turkey Hill, calling it likely too low, while pushing the committee to commit to a renovate-or-rebuild direction.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to place a special reserve fund for unbudgeted out-of-district special education and transportation costs on the November town meeting warrant.
A separate warrant article seeking additional Chapter 70 funding, an amount as heard, was withdrawn in favor of pursuing it through the regular FY27 budget process.
The committee approved two new paraprofessional positions and restoring a full-time IT support position, both drawn from the salary reserve line.
A proposal for an outside comprehensive audit of FY25 finances, funded from returned free cash, was deferred pending talks with the town manager.
Football and soccer uniforms bought without required purchase-order approval will not be penalized retroactively; undistributed soccer uniforms will be held for next year's replacement rotation.

why_it_matters: The reserve fund is a warrant article residents will vote on at November town meeting; it would let year-end school budget surplus automatically cover special education placement and transportation costs that come in over budget.
Withdrawing the Chapter 70 warrant article means any additional state aid this year would not be spent immediately but would instead be weighed against other priorities in the FY27 budget process.

The unauthorized uniform purchases and the salary-reserve-funded hires prompted the committee to signal it will develop a policy requiring pre-approval before staff spend outside the certified budget.

budget_items.what_was_said: The agreement's insurance clause for MART was holdover language never actually charged; town staff said it was a cleanup, not a substantive change.

budget_items.topic: DPW snow/ice: own equipment vs. hiring out
budget_items.what_was_said: Bill Bernard said an analysis showed it is cheaper to use town equipment and operators than to hire private vendors, based on the cost of the highest-paid heavy equipment operator.
The DPW director plans to request a new CDL-class dump truck in this year's capital request, noting the price has risen sharply since he first priced the same truck in 2022.
The DPW director said the department has run a deficit in the snow and ice budget over the last five years and plans a 2.5% annual increase to reduce, but not eliminate, it.
Failure to comply with the federal MS4 stormwater permit could carry penalties, though the director does not expect the town would actually be fined that amount.
The DPW director said the plan is a flat annual fee for residential properties, with a sliding scale for businesses based on impervious surface.

budget_items.topic: Storm water utility revenue target vs. current spending
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW director said the target is to collect roughly a set amount annually through the new utility, well above what the current storm water/drainage budget spends.
The DPW director gave a preliminary multi-year capital outlook covering equipment replacement and drainage/bridge engineering and construction.

budget_items.topic: Cost difference if storm water utility is not enacted
budget_items.what_was_said: The director said drainage and storm water line items would need to be higher in FY28 and FY29 if the utility is not approved, compared with if it is.
The DPW director said he assumed the typical annual Chapter 90 amount going forward, not the doubled amount received this year, because it is uncertain whether the increase continues.
A board member asked whether fair share money promised when voters supported the tax would continue; the DPW director said that was uncertain.

budget_items.topic: TCP building revolving account deficit closeout
budget_items.what_was_said: Officials recalled a one-time payment made at special town meeting to zero out a negative TCP revolving fund balance that had built up because the building had no real operating budget.
The facilities director said TCP's gas bill has historically run around a certain amount and he is projecting roughly half that as the building is partially decommissioned.
The facilities director restored the cleaning contract budget to its FY25 level after issues with the cleaning contractor.

budget_items.topic: TCP expense line / lost rent offset
budget_items.what_was_said: A line was added back to the facilities budget to cover the loss of rent revenue after the extended day program left the TCP building.

budget_items.topic: Food pantry electricity use at TCP
budget_items.what_was_said: The facilities director estimated the food pantry's refrigeration equipment accounts for a large share of TCP's electric cost, with an equipment-rated estimate versus a measured range.

The facilities director said he has not fully estimated the abatement cost for the decommissioned half of the TCP building but would not be surprised if it reached a certain figure; this would be requested as a capital item.
The facilities director noted the building now carries a commercial internet cost, mainly for the public access studio, higher than he expected.

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept. FY27 salary increase for 4th shift
budget_items.what_was_said: The fire chief said the salary increase reflects three step-two firefighter paramedics and one promotion to lieutenant, based on the current collective bargaining agreement.
The chief said overtime would rise due to additional time off accrued by new staff and a higher overtime rate under the new work-week schedule.
Holiday pay would increase to cover three additional staff and a higher average overtime rate.
The chief summarized the combined increase across hiring and overtime lines needed to fund a fourth shift.

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept. benefits (OPEB) cost of new hires

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept. total requested expense-line increase

budget_items.topic: Police lockup costs / Worcester County Sheriff program

meetings.headline: FY25 school budget surplus of roughly $600K traced largely to a grant line double-budgeted, unspent
meetings.summary: The School Committee reviewed a reconciled FY25 budget surplus, with the business manager and superintendent explaining it stemmed mainly from a paraprofessional line double-budgeted against a grant plus general underspending on maintenance, custodial and instructional lines, none of which affected the separate cuts made for FY26. Extensive public and committee questioning pressed on accountability, Munis reporting reliability, and the need for regular budget-to-actual reporting and backup support for the business manager going forward. The committee also worked through a draft FY27 capital plan, debating how to finance a needed turf field/track replacement alongside a possible solar revenue project, and took votes on line-item transfers, a music program donation, a grant application, new legal counsel, and added secretarial hours at the high school.

meetings.summary: The School Committee's meeting centered on a newly discovered FY25 budget surplus of roughly $582,000 (about 2% of the budget), far above the district's normal cushion, which the chair and later the business manager attributed to poor financial oversight rather than known wrongdoing. The committee approved FY25 line-item transfers and a warrant, heard the superintendent's and building principals' start-of-year reports (including the first-day fire at the middle/high school), reviewed an FY27 budget timeline, and discussed a possible best-practices/forensic audit, a stabilization fund for out-of-district special education placements, and extra Chapter 70 money for a fall town meeting warrant article; several residents used public comment to press for accountability and clearer FY25-vs-FY26 budget transparency.

The committee voted to approve five FY25 line-item transfers, shifting money between accounts including athletics, stipends, and building maintenance to cover shortfalls.

meetings.headline: Health insurance costs projected to rise about $1 million over three years, pushing talk of opt-out and GIC alternatives
meetings.summary: This joint select board/finance committee/school committee session was a night of preliminary FY27 budget presentations rather than votes: Council on Aging, the library, health insurance, board of health, veteran services, band concerts, and the historic commission each presented before the boards. The heaviest discussion was health insurance, where a three-year projection showed costs climbing sharply, prompting debate over the PEC's opt-out program, plan design, and whether to explore the state's GIC plan; smaller line items (band concerts, veteran services reimbursement) drew pointed questions about oversight and financial reporting that were left for follow-up rather than resolved.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. reconciliation.coverage: official minutes are a summary only

The one thing a reader should check is the Historic Commission item: our recording captured a discussion of a separate $5,000 line meant for an APDC hero-banner transfer that the official minutes never mention at all, while dozens of other precise dollar figures (library trust funds, health-insurance cost breakdowns, veteran-services history) that our captions caught simply never made it into the official narrative summary.

budget_items.what_was_said: Warrants covering May 6 through May 16, 2025 were reported for the chair to sign; the committee does not vote on warrants, only line-item transfers.
The committee authorized annual funding for student activity accounts at each school, unchanged from prior years.
The Senate bill to study the Chapter 70 formula includes a state appropriation for a consultant to support the commission's work.
The letter to the legislature will note the number of positions and FTEs cut from the district's permanent staff and the share this represents.
The adopted bus fee policy sets annual per-student fees, reduced rates for reduced-lunch status, no fee for free-lunch status, and family caps for multiple children.
The new superintendent's contract includes dues for a national superintendents' association membership.

decisions.decision: Member questions to central office staff should be copied to the chair so the chair is aware of recurring issues, within open meeting law limits.
Committee will email the town manager and the chairs of the select board and finance committee to gauge interest in a November special town meeting FY27 override.
Superintendent will provide the committee with a level-services FY27/FY28 budget projection incorporating already-settled bus and teacher/para contracts, before the last meeting of the year.
Level-services budget comparisons will exclude positions funded by free cash, since that funding is one-time and outside the regular budget.
A member will contact assistant town manager Jen Warren to ask how other towns have handled/broken out health insurance in departmental budgets, for comparison purposes.
The committee will proceed with the superintendent's contract as originally negotiated and signed, rather than adopt the attorney's later red-lined revisions or renegotiate.

meetings.summary: This special meeting was a 75-minute, 13-question interview of Joanie Manard, the finalist candidate for superintendent of schools, covering her background, budgeting philosophy, leadership style, student safety approach, staffing and hiring practices, and community relationships. No vote was taken on the candidacy itself; the committee adjourned by roll-call vote and set deliberations for the following day, and reminded the community it could submit feedback via survey.

budget_items.what_was_said: Candidate described sitting on every budget subcommittee meeting in her current district and involving staff from the classroom level up in budget recommendations. No dollar figures were given.
Candidate said capital expenses, unlike the regular operating budget, should be projected further out to schedule roofing, building and curriculum-review cycles.
A member asked whether a public-facing, manipulable budget could be ready for the launch of the next school year; the candidate said yes, with frantic summer work.

Candidate described grants she oversees being approved, then unapproved, then approved again amid federal changes including the discussed dismantling of a cabinet department of education. No figures were cited.

budget_items.what_was_said: Discussion of hiring practices intended to find teachers who can also coach or run extracurriculars, addressing budget pressure to have staff cover multiple needs. No figures were given.

meetings.headline: School Committee interviewed superintendent finalist Timothy McCormack for 75 minutes; no hiring decision made
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee held a special meeting to conduct a 75-minute, 13-question finalist interview for superintendent with candidate Timothy McCormack, currently superintendent in North Brookfield. Questions covered his background, budget philosophy, hiring practices, student safety, staff culture, labor relations, a past personal-conduct disclosure, and handling of a Facebook controversy over a Turkey Hill hire; the meeting ended with McCormack's closing statement and a roll-call vote to adjourn, with no hiring decision made.

budget_items.what_was_said: A committee member asked how the candidate would reconcile adding new programs with the district having just had to cut its budget, noting the figure is now lower than first thought.
The candidate described state grant funding attached to the Project Lead the Way / STEM pathway, paid in an initial larger amount and smaller amounts in subsequent years.
The candidate said his district received grant funding from the 18 Foundation to support programs like Project Lead the Way.

budget_items.topic: Value of a high school diploma vs. college
budget_items.what_was_said: A committee member challenged the candidate on steering some students away from college, citing average earnings for a high school diploma holder.

budget_items.topic: Cost differential in hiring a more experienced teacher
budget_items.what_was_said: The candidate discussed hiring a more expensive, experienced candidate versus a cheaper one, saying a district must find budget room elsewhere if it pays more for a position.
The candidate said conversations with the finance committee have grown more difficult as the required share of net school spending covered by the town has dropped sharply.
The candidate said his current district saw a reduction in rural school aid for next year that a slight increase in Chapter 70 would not fully offset.
The candidate said losing this funding, which had subsidized salaries, forced hard decisions about which positions were needs versus nice-to-haves.
The candidate referenced roughly twenty-plus one-to-one or small-group instructional aides in his district and the ongoing need to support them.

budget_items.what_was_said: Conway said Lunenburg's state aid has been declining, shifting more of the cost to local taxpayers, and compared it to Pentucket's own decline in state aid share over ten years.

budget_items.topic: Pentucket budget gap closed via new revenue
budget_items.what_was_said: Conway described facing a budget gap at Pentucket that was closed partly by raising revenue through summer programming, expanded preschool, and increased facility rental income.
Conway said putting the transportation contract out to competitive bid brought the three-year contract cost down sharply once a competitor entered the bidding.
Conway called health insurance a major budget driver, citing recent rate increases well above typical assumed growth rates.
Conway explained that an approved September budget commonly looks different by year-end because of line transfers made to respond to changing needs, such as adding a kindergarten class.
Conway said UGGA has remained largely flat and argued that if it kept pace with Chapter 70 growth the town would have more budget flexibility.
Conway described a robotics program he built at Pentucket that runs on an annual budget funded largely by industry sponsorships and grants rather than district funds.

budget_items.what_was_said: Conway noted the schools' share of the town budget rose after last year's override and is coming back down, and cited other towns' target school/town budget split ratios as points of comparison.

budget_items.what_was_said: The House Ways and Means budget raised minimum Chapter 70 aid per student from the governor's figure, but a member cautioned this could still change in the Senate and reconciliation.
The House budget fully funded charter school reimbursement at this rate, though a member said that isn't guaranteed to hold.
The House budget proposed this reimbursement rate for required out-of-district placement transportation, prorated based on available funds.
A one-time supplemental appropriations bill drawing on fair share tax surplus was finalized and referred to the Senate.
The supplemental bill raised FY25 regional school transportation reimbursement from the prior rate to full reimbursement.
FY25 circuit breaker reimbursement for out-of-district special education transportation costs was increased from a lower rate.

budget_items.topic: FY26 out-of-district special ed transportation reimbursement

The chair said a state representative and the select board chair both reported this amount in earmarks for Lunenburg public schools.
Warrants covering late March to mid-April were presented to the committee for approval.
A donation for STEM supplies at the primary school was recommended for deposit into the school gift account.
An anonymous donation to help students attend Nature's Classroom was recommended for deposit into the Turkey Hill gift account.

budget_items.what_was_said: The transfer was proposed to cover anticipated Canon copier lease and per-copy billing; the business manager said usage caps are being studied but not yet implemented.

budget_items.topic: Transfer: fire safety/furniture repair to vehicle maintenance repair
budget_items.what_was_said: The transfer was requested to cover a deficit in vehicle repair/maintenance for truck and mower repairs through year end.
Money held in the salary reserve line from prior-year bargaining was being dispersed to appropriate salary lines, as is done annually.

Funds were moved into athletic transportation, special detail/events, dues and fees, and high school stipend lines to address a deficit in the athletics revolving account; more reclassification was still expected.
The district switched vendors for Chromebook repair parts after the usual vendor's pricing rose sharply due to tariffs, raising concern about the FY26 budget.
Food service will sell bagged lunches at annual town meeting with several sandwich options, cash only.

budget_items.topic: Potential position restorations from pending state funding
budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent estimated that if pending state funding bills all passed, the district could restore about this many positions.
One option discussed was raising the student activity fee to cover advisor stipend costs, with free/reduced-lunch students automatically waived.
Fee calculations were based on the portion of enrollment not eligible for the automatic fee waiver.
A committee member noted the activity fee was set at this amount in 2008, much lower than the current proposal.

budget_items.topic: Municipal building / school district offices project cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The presenter cited the overall project value used in pricing calculations for the town hall, Ritter building and meeting house work.

budget_items.topic: Turkey Hill full renovation vs. replacement cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The architect estimated the cost to address everything identified in the Turkey Hill study, versus a rough cost to build an entirely new school.
The mechanical engineer said a required fire sprinkler system would cost roughly this amount regardless of which HVAC option is chosen.

budget_items.topic: Turkey Hill HVAC options cost range
budget_items.what_was_said: The engineer outlined a range of costs across three HVAC strategy options, from a basic repair approach to full electrification.
The outdated electrical system would need to be upgraded no matter which overall option is chosen.

budget_items.topic: Turkey Hill total study cost estimate
budget_items.what_was_said: The total estimate to address everything identified in the report was given, described as less than expected and far less than a new building.

budget_items.topic: Turkey Hill roof and window costs / MSBA reimbursement
budget_items.what_was_said: The architect gave rough costs for window and roof work and said MSBA reimbursement might cover roughly half if the town pursued the program.
The committee discussed how to prioritize use of free cash for FY26, following up on the prior meeting's conversation.

budget_items.topic: Restoring part athletic director/assistant principal and secretary
budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent proposed combining a reduced assistant principal role with athletic director duties and restoring a part-time secretary using free cash.

budget_items.topic: Athletic director salary offset from athletic revolving fund
budget_items.what_was_said: The FY26 budget already offsets part of the athletic director's salary from the athletic revolving account; the superintendent hoped this could balance out as the revolving fund's health improves.

budget_items.topic: Title I and special education federal grants at risk
budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent said roughly this total in federal Title I and special education grant money was at risk pending a federal certification dispute over DEI practices, and proposed free cash as a backstop.
The green-communities-grant-funded mini-split project at the primary school had a funding shortfall the superintendent proposed covering with free cash.

The superintendent estimated potential unemployment costs from the budget cuts and proposed adding to the existing unemployment budget line with free cash, while expecting the full estimate would not be needed.
A member noted the existing budget already includes an increase intended to help attract a qualified finance/business manager candidate.
Opening additional school choice seats across several grades was projected to generate this much potential revenue the following fiscal year, plus a Chapter 70 effect.
The town manager's warrant article sought to cover FY2025 and prior-year operating deficits, including unanticipated special education move-ins.
The article included funds to decommission portions of the TC Pasios building.
A citizens petition proposition 2½ override question to supplement the school budget was on the warrant; the committee ultimately declined to take a position.

budget_items.topic: Article 12 - Free cash supplement to school operating budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The article would supplement the FY26 school operating budget using free cash, consistent with the earlier discussion.
The parks commission described a scaled-back two-phase project and cited differing per-household cost estimates for the proposed debt exclusion.

budget_items.what_was_said: The total project cost for the Ritter building, town hall and annex renovation, including design fees and contingency, was presented for the debt exclusion article.

Declining to take a position on the citizens' petition override leaves that budget question to town meeting without a School Committee recommendation either way.

meetings.headline: Committee voted to swap FY26 capital projects for funds to finish a grant-funded mini-split project
meetings.summary: An emergency school committee meeting was called to decide whether to amend the FY26 capital plan, pulling several school capital projects (playground and driveway design studies, safety window film, and a Turkey Hill hot water tank replacement, among others) and replacing them with funding to complete phase two of the mini-split installation at the primary school, in order to use a Green Communities grant before it expires and free the town to apply for further grants. After extended discussion about the funding math, the abruptness of the request, and tradeoffs against deferred safety projects, the committee voted by roll call to endorse the town manager's and superintendent's plan to modify the capital plan request.

what_happened.line: A citizen-petitioned override that would add funding to the FY26 schools budget, contingent on a townwide ballot vote, was discussed at length with no vote taken on the override itself.
The committee was told that after FY25 and FY26 cuts, the district will have fewer staff positions than it had five years ago.

The committee also voted to accept a multi-year salary schedule for unaffiliated staff and the FY26 school calendar.

why_it_matters: The override is a Proposition 2 1/2 ballot question that would raise additional funds for the schools budget beyond the town manager's proposal; a yes or no vote will fall to town voters.
The staffing comparison speaks to what programs and support the district can offer next year, including the special education and music positions named in public comment.
The quarterly transfers move existing appropriated funds between budget lines and do not change the total amount raised.

meetings.headline: School Committee passed a deeply-cut FY26 budget and created Lunenburg's first student transportation fee.
meetings.summary:
The School Committee worked through the superintendent's FY26 recommended budget line by line, confirming a Director of Finance restructuring, a cut to one of two curriculum coaches, and rejecting a proposed librarian cut, while extensive public comment focused on athletic and band cuts, the co-op ski program's cost, and equity between academics and extracurriculars. The committee voted to table a ski program cut pending renegotiation with partner schools, adopted a new student bus fee (with rates and a waiver policy sent to the policy subcommittee) to help offset transportation costs, and ultimately passed the FY26 budget unanimously with the ski program retained and funded by projected bus fee revenue; members also confirmed they will not pursue a school override this year in favor of a possible townwide override next year.</summary>
</invoke>

The committee set proposed bus fee rates for one child, two-or-more children, and a reduced rate, to be sent to the policy subcommittee for a waiver policy.

The committee agreed to cut one of two curriculum coach positions rather than both, with the district's curriculum director absorbing some duties for the eliminated role.
A proposal to cut a librarian position was rejected by consensus as librarians were described as already stretched across schools and responsible for a full curriculum block.

decisions.decision: Following a joint meeting with the Select Board the night before, the school committee reached consensus not to pursue a school-specific override this year, favoring a future townwide override instead.
Consensus not to cut a librarian position from the budget.
Consensus to cut one of two curriculum coach positions, not both.
Consensus to pursue a shuttle/carpool arrangement for Reggie Lewis Center track trips rather than a sport-specific fee, and to consider a small general transportation fee increase instead.
Directed the athletic director to attempt to renegotiate cost-sharing for the co-op ski program with partner schools before any decision to cut it.
Directed staff to bring clarity, before the next meeting, on how any free cash allocation to the schools would structurally be handled at town meeting.

Decided not to restore the fifth-grade teacher position at this meeting given funding uncertainty, per the superintendent's recommendation against relying on projected bus-fee or free-cash revenue for a position.

meetings.headline: Committee raised athletic and facility fees to help close a deep FY26 budget gap forcing likely staff cuts.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee spent most of a long meeting confronting a severe FY26 budget shortfall driven by inflation, rising special education and transportation costs, and state Chapter 70 aid not keeping pace, with public and committee comment repeatedly blaming inadequate state funding and past reluctance to override. The committee voted to raise athletic fees and facility rental rates, tabled proposed transportation and student-activity fee changes, walked through a long menu of possible administrative, staffing and program cuts, and took public budget questions; a member also announced he will resign in May.

meetings.headline: FY26 budget gap forces deep proposed staff cuts, hitting young grades and special education hardest
meetings.summary: The school committee handled routine business (minutes, grants, a track-and-field warrant article, facility contracts, a competency determination, and a revised superintendent search adding external candidates) before spending most of the meeting on a grim FY26 budget presentation: to meet the town manager's target the district would cut dozens of teaching, paraprofessional, counseling and support positions, with the deepest impact on elementary grades and special education. No budget vote was taken; the committee instead gave feedback, discussed alternative revenue and staffing ideas, and heard extensive public comment expressing alarm about the proposed cuts and frustration with state Chapter 70 funding.

what_happened.line: School Committee voted 3-0 to approve the internal job posting for Superintendent of Lunenburg Public Schools.
School Committee voted 3-0 to authorize a call for a 12-person screening committee to help run the search.
The votes followed a closed executive session on non-union personnel matters, with no public comment offered either before or after.
The committee chose not to reserve specific seats (such as Select Board or public safety) on the screening committee, planning instead to assemble a diverse pool once applications arrive.
Members discussed a possible special meeting around January 29 to appoint the screening committee sooner and start subcommittee work in early February.

why_it_matters: This starts the process for choosing the district's next superintendent, following the current superintendent's planned retirement.
Residents interested in serving may apply to the 12-person screening committee once the call goes out, rather than being appointed to a designated seat.
Salary and contract terms for the new superintendent remain open for negotiation with the school committee, not fixed by the posting.

The call for screening-committee applicants, to be posted at the library, senior center, on Facebook and the town website

not_audible: The long executive session stretch (roughly 268 to 1631 seconds) has no substantive captions, only repeated placeholder text.
The exact total of the December 16-19, 2024 warrants is garbled in the captions (rendered as "$237,000 2027 237,000 271").
The facilities revolving account (Munis) ending balance is garbled, rendered variously as "$1,359" and "$359" in the same passage.
The full name of the donor introduced as "George" (surname heard as "wer") is not clearly rendered.

Several speakers are not clearly identified by name in the captions, including the person presenting the transportation contract update and a person addressed as "Peter" and "Kate" whose exact roles are not stated.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.coverage: official minutes are a summary only
reconciliation.summary: The two records agree on the outcome of every vote that appears in both, and on the handful of figures the official minutes bother to state (warrant total, donation amounts, the $300,000 Turkey Hill door capital, FY24 free cash), but the official minutes omit nearly all the numeric and procedural detail our caption-derived minutes captured — the withdrawn transportation motion, the ARPA transfer, and virtually every athletic-finance and revolving-account figure. The one thing a reader should actually check is the Vincent Joseph scholarship: our minutes give $115,000 (heard twice, at the vote and in the figures) against the official minutes' $15,000 — a $100,000 gap on the same named gift that is too large to be a digit-grouping slip.

what_happened.line: Superintendent Burnham announced her retirement at the end of the school year, and the committee appointed a two-member search subcommittee.
The committee took no vote on a restructured athletic fee proposal, choosing to gather public and booster feedback before deciding nearer the budget vote.
Dr. Gilson was authorized to negotiate and finalize a renegotiated transportation contract after an initial bid came in with a steep first-year increase.
The department will send the town's building design committee written objection to placing the ACE special education program in a basement-level space.
A phase-one door and security award was approved at Turkey Hill, with full door replacement deferred pending state (MSBA) guidance.

why_it_matters: A superintendent search will shape district leadership heading into next school year, and residents will see subcommittee updates as it proceeds.
The undecided athletic fee proposal will factor into the FY budget residents vote on, once public and booster feedback is gathered.
Where the ACE special education program is housed in the planned joint municipal building affects students and families relying on that program.
